newsitem.title: VIRGIN ISLANDS: Clinton reads, relaxes in the Virgin Islands.
newsitem.headline: Clinton reads, relaxes in the Virgin Islands.

text.p: President Bill Clinton relaxed on Thursday in the sunny splendor of the Virgin Islands and promptly turned his thoughts to Ireland -- in fact and fiction.

Resting at a spacious adobe-style villa overlooking the azure waters of Megan's Bay with his wife Hillary and daughter Chelsea, Clinton opted for a low-key start to his first full day on the hilly Caribbean island of St. Thomas.
Instead of visiting the sites that lure tourists to this vacation mecca, Clinton explored recent Irish history.

"The president brought with him two books," said Deputy White House Press Secretary Mary Ellen Glynn. One of them was "The Greening of the White House", by Irish Times reporter Conor O'Clery, which traces Clinton's role in shifting U.S. policy toward seeking peace in Northern Ireland.

The book was released in Ireland last month and will be available in the United States in March. It traces Clinton's actions to further Irish peace moves, beginning with his decision to change long-standing U.S. policy and allow Gerry Adams, head of Sinn Fein, the Irish Republican Army's political wing, to visit the United States. This was seen as helping in the 1994 declaration of an IRA ceasefire.
Clinton also became the first U.S. president to visit Northern Ireland in November 1995.
The president also brought with him the latest novel by best-selling author Andrew Greeley, who uses Ireland and Chicago as the settings for "Irish Lace."
Glynn said Clinton described the book as being "about two of my favorite places, Chicago and Ireland."
When not reading, Clinton had the use of a private beach to take advantage of the the warm, clear waters surrounding the Island. A trip to a topless beach nearby was not in the offing.

"After a long campaign and a long month of November and December where he went on a foreign trip and then picked his Cabinet and some of his top White House staff ... he's going to take at least these three days to relax" before the stresses of Washington resume, Glynn said.

Shortly after winning a second term in November, Clinton went on a 12-day trip to the Pacific Rim that included stops in Australia, the Philippines and Thailand. He then wrestled with decision about reshaping his Cabinet and filling top White House posts before taking the oath of office on Jan. 20.

Clinton, who plans to return to Washinton on Sunday, has scheduled a "Cabinet retreat" for the following weekend at a site yet to be decided, Glynn said. Four years ago, Clinton held such a retreat at Camp David to develop a "team spirit" among senior officials of his administration.

Once Clinton returns to Washington, he will work on his Inaugural address, which sets out a president's goals and objective for the next four years. In early February he presents his budget for the next fiscal year to Congress and delivers the annual State of the Union address to the nation.

The Clintons arrived in the Virgin Islands on Wednesday, after ushering in the New Year at Hilton Head, South Carolina, at the annual "Renaissance Weekend," an invitation-only gathering of some 1,500 people that the president and his wife have attended for more than a decade.
